name: Electric spot-reducer

lead: The Electric Spot Reducer was an electric massager advertised in mid-century magazines and comic books, sold by the Spot Reducer Co. of Newark, New Jersey. Ads promised that using it on hips, abdomen and other areas would take off fat and inches without exercise or strict dieting.

Its appeal was a slimmer silhouette from massage alone. Spot reduction, the idea that working one area removes fat there, is rejected by researchers, and a 1959 Post Office proceeding reviewed the advertising claims.

paras: Buyers ordered by mail, often sending a small trial payment, and held the vibrating unit against problem areas for a few minutes at a time as in the ads. A 10-day home trial with a money-back guarantee was part of the offer.

The main documented issue was the advertising: the Post Office judicial officer found the claims went beyond medical advice the seller received. Massagers of this type are generally low risk in use, but buyers could pay for a result the device did not deliver.

chain: Vibrating massager applied to a chosen area
angle.text: The device was sold as a way to slim particular areas through massage. Four physicians testified in the 1959 proceeding that massage alone does not meaningfully change weight or measurements [1].

lead: The Electric Spot Reducer was a mail-order electric massager sold in the late 1940s and 1950s by the Spot Reducer Co. of Newark, New Jersey, whose president was Joseph H. Pinkus [1]. It was sold at prices of $2.00, $9.95 and $12.95 and advertised for slimming specific body areas [1].

The pitch was visual: lose weight and fat where it shows, without exercise or a strict diet, with a 10-day home trial and a money-back guarantee [1]. The product belonged to a wave of mid-century reducing machines and vibrating belts that promised local slimming.

In a tentative decision dated February 6, 1959, a US Post Office judicial officer found that the advertising conveyed that the device alone would reduce weight and fat, and that it could not do so, concluding a fraud order should issue [1]. Fitness research generally holds that fat is lost across the whole body through diet and exercise rather than from one targeted spot [2].

paras: Advertisements stated or implied that the device used alone would reduce weight and fat in specific body areas, with results promised without exercise or strict diet and a 10-day trial offered [1]. The complaint was later amended to cover the name Body Massager [1].

Four physicians for the complainant testified that massage alone does not produce meaningful weight or fat reduction and reported no significant change in weight or measurements in their tests. Four physicians for the respondent gave views ranging from the device assisting weight loss to mainly changing measurements, though their tests were generally not diet-free. The officer found the complainant's experts represented the prevailing medical view and found intent to deceive. The charge that refunds were withheld was not proven [1].
Studies of spot reduction report that exercising one body part does not reduce fat in that area; one study of tennis players found more muscle but no less subcutaneous fat in the dominant arm [2].
No studies found on this specific device beyond the physician testimony recorded in the 1959 proceeding [1].

timeline.event: Comic-book and magazine ads for the Electric Spot Reducer circulate.
US Post Office tentative decision (Feb 6) concludes a fraud order should issue against Spot Reducer Co. [1].
